summary: This informational document specifies how to carry Kerberos V5 over TLS for extra security features. The Kerberos messages travel through a TLS connection. It is not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Kerberos tickets are encrypted, but the conversation that obtains them is not, so someone in the middle can talk a client into using weak encryption. This memo describes a way to run the whole Kerberos exchange inside a TLS connection, so that the negotiation itself cannot be tampered with.

questions: what is the kerberos-tls srv record
subtitle: How a Kerberos client and its KDC can upgrade their TCP connection to TLS for privacy and extra authentication.

tldr.problem: Plain Kerberos V5 leaves parts of its messages unprotected, and an active attacker can use that to force a weak encryption type or a broken pre-authentication method.
tldr.mechanism: The client asks for the STARTTLS extension in the Kerberos TCP extension bitmask, the server answers, and the client then runs a TLS handshake on the same connection before any Kerberos message is exchanged.
tldr.outcome: The Kerberos exchange then runs inside the protected channel, which stops downgrade attacks and hides the names and lifetimes that plain Kerberos exposes, at the cost of a certificate check that the document leaves optional for constrained clients.

today: RFC 6251 is an Informational document from May 2011, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes it and none that updates it. It describes an extension to the Kerberos TCP mechanism rather than a change to Kerberos itself, so a client and a server both have to support it before it can be used.

sections.title: Why Put Kerberos Inside TLS
sections.content:
The document describes how a Kerberos V5 (RFC 4120) implementation may upgrade communication between clients and Key Distribution Centers to use the Transport Layer Security protocol (RFC 5246). TLS offers integrity- and privacy-protected exchanges that can be authenticated using X.509 certificates, OpenPGP keys (RFC 6091), and usernames and passwords via Secure Remote Password (RFC 5054).

There are several reasons to use Kerberos V5 over TLS. The first is that it prevents downgrade attacks affecting, for example, encryption types and pre-authentication data negotiation. The encryption type field in the KDC-REQ and the METHOD-DATA field with the requested pre-authentication types, sent by the server in KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED errors in the KDC-REP, are sent without integrity or privacy protection in Kerberos V5. That allows an active attacker to replace the encryption type with a compromised one, such as 56-bit DES, or to request that clients use a broken pre-authentication type. Since clients in general cannot know which encryption types other servers support, or which pre-authentication types servers prefer or require, it is difficult for the client to detect whether there was a man in the middle or whether the remote server simply did not support a stronger encryption type or preferred another pre-authentication type.

The second reason is that Kerberos exchanges are not wholly privacy protected. Parts of many Kerberos packets are transferred without encryption, and that part contains information such as the client principal name, the server principal name, the encryption types supported by the client and the lifetime of tickets. Revealing such information is, in some threat models, considered a problem.

The third reason is that it provides additional authentication against the KDC. In some situations users are equipped with smart cards holding an RSA authentication key, and in others they have an OpenPGP client on their desktop with a public key known to the server. The fourth is that it provides explicit server authentication of the KDC to the client: in traditional Kerberos V5, authentication of the KDC is proved as a side effect of the KDC knowing your encryption key, that is, your password.
sections.plainLanguage: Kerberos encrypts the tickets it hands out, but the first conversation, where the client and the server agree on how strong to be, is out in the open. Someone in the middle can rewrite that agreement and talk the client into using an encryption type that is no longer safe. Wrapping the conversation in TLS closes that gap, and it also hides who is asking for what.

sections.title: The STARTTLS Extension
sections.content:
The STARTTLS extension uses the Kerberos V5 TCP extension mechanism (RFC 5021), and uses bit 0 in the extension bitmask. The protocol is as follows. The client requests the extension by setting the STARTTLS bit in the TCP extension mechanism bitmask; how to deal with extension negotiation failures at this point is described in RFC 5021. After the server has sent the 4-octet value 0x00000000 to indicate support of this extension, the stream is controlled by the TLS protocol and its framing. The TLS protocol is initiated by the client.

Typically the client initiates the TLS handshake protocol by sending a client hello, the server responds, and the handshake continues until it either succeeds or fails. If for any reason the handshake fails, the STARTTLS protocol also fails and the TLS error is used as the error indication. In that case no further messages can be exchanged over the same TCP session.

If the handshake succeeds, the Kerberos V5 authentication protocol is performed within the protected TLS channel, like a normal TCP Kerberos V5 exchange. In particular, every Kerberos V5 packet will be prefixed by a 4-octet length field that indicates the length of the Kerberos V5 packet. When no further Kerberos V5 messages need to be transferred in the TLS session, the TLS session MUST be shut down properly using the close_notify alert. When the TLS session is shut down, the TCP connection cannot be reused to send any further data and MUST be closed.
sections.plainLanguage: The upgrade happens on the same TCP connection the Kerberos exchange would have used. The client asks for it, the server confirms, and from then on the connection belongs to TLS. If the handshake fails the exchange is over, because the connection cannot be reused. Once it works, the Kerberos messages look exactly as they do over plain TCP, with a length prefix, but they are now inside the encrypted channel.

sections.title: Finding a KDC That Supports It
sections.content:
Section 7.2.3 of Kerberos V5 (RFC 4120) describes how Domain Name System SRV records (RFC 2782) can be used to find the address of a KDC. This document defines a new service of kerberos-tls to indicate that the particular KDC is intended to support the STARTTLS extension. The Proto, Realm, TTL, Class, SRV, Priority, Weight, Port and Target have the same meaning as in RFC 4120.

The example given in the document is a pair of SRV records for the service name kerberos-tls over TCP in the realm EXAMPLE.COM, pointing at two different KDC hosts on port 88, with different priorities and weights.
sections.plainLanguage: A client that wants the extra protection has to find a server that offers it, and the existing way of finding Kerberos servers is DNS. So the memo adds a second service name, kerberos-tls, published in the same way, which says: these servers support the upgrade.

sections.title: Server Certificates
sections.content:
The TLS protocol may be used in a mode that provides server authentication using, for example, X.509 and OpenPGP. A goal for the protocol is that it should be as easy to implement and deploy on clients as support for UDP or TCP. Since many client environments do not have access to long-term storage, or to long-term storage that is sufficiently secure to enable validation of server certificates, the Kerberos V5 STARTTLS protocol does not require clients to verify server certificates. If server certification had been required, environments with constrained clients would be forced to disable TLS, which would arguably be worse than TLS without server certificate validation, since the use of TLS even without server certificate validation protects against some attacks that Kerberos V5 over UDP or TCP does not. For example, even without server certificate validation, TLS protects against passive network sniffing aimed at tracking Kerberos service usage by a given client.

The use of TLS without server certificate verification does, however, open up a range of active attacks such as man in the middle. When clients have the ability, they MUST validate the server certificate. For this reason, if a KDC presents an X.509 server certificate over TLS, it MUST contain an otherName Subject Alternative Name identified using a type id of id-krb5starttls-san. The intention is to bind the server certificate to the Kerberos realm for the purpose of using Kerberos V5 STARTTLS, and the value field of the otherName should contain the realm as the Realm ASN.1 type.

To validate a server certificate, the client MAY use local configuration, for example a list that maps the Kerberos realm to a copy of the server's certificate, and compare that with the authentication information provided by the server via TLS. The server certificate could be an X.509 certificate or an OpenPGP key, and in this mode the client needs no processing related to id-krb5starttls-san. When the server presents an X.509 server certificate, clients MAY use Certification Path Validation as described in RFC 5280 to validate it. In addition, unless the client can otherwise verify that the server certificate is bound to the KDC of the target realm, the client MUST verify that the certificate contains the id-krb5starttls-san alternative name and that the value is identical to the intended Kerberos realm.
sections.plainLanguage: The document makes certificate checking optional, because many clients have nowhere safe to keep a copy of the server's key. A client that cannot check the certificate gets protection against passive snooping but not against an active attacker. A client that can check it must, and the certificate has to name the realm in a dedicated field.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations in Kerberos V5, TLS and the Kerberos V5 TCP extension mechanism are inherited. TLS does not protect against man-in-the-middle attacks unless clients verify the KDC's credentials, such as an X.509 certificate or an OpenPGP key, correctly. Although certificate validation adds an extra layer of protection, that is not considered strictly necessary to improve the security profile of Kerberos V5 as outlined in this document.

If server authentication is used, some information about the server, such as its name, is visible to passive attackers. To protect against the inherent downgrade attack in the extension framework, implementations SHOULD offer a policy mode that requires this extension to always be successfully negotiated, for a particular realm or generally. For interoperability with implementations that do not support the extension, the policy mode SHOULD be disabled by default.
sections.plainLanguage: Two points to keep in mind. TLS only stops a man in the middle if the client checks who it is talking to. And because the extension itself is negotiated, an attacker could try to make the negotiation fail; a client that can be told to insist on the extension closes that door, though the memo leaves that setting off by default so that older servers still work.

data.code:

viz.caption: THE FOUR REASONS GIVEN FOR USING KERBEROS OVER TLS

items.title: No downgrade attacks
items.text: The choice of encryption type and pre-authentication type can no longer be rewritten in transit.

items.title: Privacy for the negotiation
items.text: Principal names, supported encryption types and ticket lifetimes are no longer visible on the wire.

items.title: Extra authentication of the client
items.text: The KDC can also check a smart card key or an OpenPGP key.

items.title: Explicit authentication of the KDC
items.text: The server proves who it is with a certificate, rather than only by knowing your password.
